title: Judging LLMs: Alex Volkov

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central focus is LLM evaluation methodology: three evaluation methods, LLM-as-judge, custom criteria creation, and bias checking. Evaluation practices discussed apply across all AI applications without a specific vertical focus. The talk covers building evaluation pipelines during development, evaluation methodology, and production tracing concerns. Requires basic LLM and Python knowledge but is accessible to practitioners without advanced ML expertise. A conference talk delivered at the AI Engineer World's Fair, styled as a courtroom drama. Six evidence anchors directly support the evaluation methodology classification.

summary: The talk is structured as a courtroom proceeding presided over by 'Maximus,' an AGI judge from 2034, with Alex Volkov serving as human-in-the-loop commentator. Through a series of entertaining 'cases,' Volkov imparts critical lessons for AI engineers. Case 1 (Daniel R.) involves YOLO-ing a chat-with-PDF app to production without tracing, then breaking features with Friday prompt changes. Verdict: guilty of 'no trace left behind.' Lesson: trace and log everything in production—W&B Weave requires just one line of code via a Python decorator. Case 2 (Sasha S.) charges the engineer with 'premature fine-tun-itis'—jumping straight to fine-tuning Llama 3 without first iterating on prompts. Lesson: exhaust prompt engineering techniques like Chain of Thought, flow engineering, and mixture of agents before fine-tuning. Case 3 (Morgan M.) covers an engineer who stopped following AI news and stuck with Llama 2 7B. Sentence commuted to 'community service'—attending ThursdAI shows. Case 4 (Francisco I. at Air Canada) involves rushing a chatbot to production using only programmatic assertions, resulting in a lost legal battle. Volkov then provides a refresher on LLM evals: compiling a dataset of inputs with correct answers or criteria, running the model, and scoring. Three methods are detailed: (1) programmatic evaluations for numerical outputs, assertions, and code; (2) human-in-the-loop for continuous development evaluation, though costly and boring; (3) LLM-as-judge for cost-effective grading of multi-turn conversations, still requiring human iteration and bias checking. The positive case (Maxim) shows all three methods implemented correctly using W&B Weave, with continuous evaluation, fast experiments, and catching prompt regressions—though a prompt injection incident highlights the need to validate judges for biases. Volkov emphasizes creating custom evaluation criteria rather than relying on off-the-shelf ones, referencing a paper by Shankar on validating validators and a talk by Hamel Hussein. He demonstrates W&B Weave's evaluation system through OpenUI, an open-source project by W&B co-founder Chris van Pelt, showing custom criteria (contrast, relevance, polish), version comparison, and multimedia rendering. Volkov walks through a practical exercise of creating custom criteria using a conference talk as an example. The talk concludes with a humorous final case where Maxim judges Alex himself—guilty of 'over commitment to the bit' for his courtroom theatrics, including wearing a wig on stage.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Always trace and log everything in production—W&B Weave requires just one Python decorator to start
Iterate on prompts before fine-tuning; use Chain of Thought, flow engineering, mixture of agents first
Keep up with rapid AI model releases; resources like the ThursdAI weekly podcast help filter the noise
Don't rely solely on programmatic assertions in production; human-in-the-loop evaluation is essential
Three main LLM evaluation methods: programmatic, human-in-the-loop, and LLM-as-judge, each with distinct trade-offs
LLM-as-judge is cost-effective but still requires human iteration, bias checking, and custom criteria creation
Create custom evaluation criteria specific to your business rather than relying on off-the-shelf ones—only you know what your app is doing
Validate your validators: check LLM judges for biases, as referenced in Shankar's paper on the topic
Build evaluation pipelines early during development, not just after production deployment
A robust evaluation system with visualization tools is essential for moving fast in LLM development

sections.title: Introduction and Court Framing
sections.summary: Alex Volkov introduces the courtroom format with 'Maximus,' an AGI judge from 2034, establishing the humorous tone and the human-in-the-loop commentary concept.

sections.title: Daniel's Case — No Trace Left Behind
sections.summary: Daniel YOLO'd a chat-with-PDF app to production, then broke existing features with Friday prompt changes without any tracing or logging. Guilty of 'no trace left behind.' W&B Weave demoed as one-line tracing solution with dashboard for call stack inspection.

sections.title: June 8 D's Case — Missed Connections
sections.summary: Brief case about an engineer who didn't buy a ticket to AI Expo 2024. Guilty of 'many connections lost.'

sections.title: Sasha's Case — Premature Fine-Tun-itis
sections.summary: Sasha fine-tuned Llama 3 on company data (6% improvement, 5e-6 learning rate) without first iterating on prompts. Guilty of 'premature fine-tun-itis.' Lesson: use prompt engineering techniques before fine-tuning. W&B Models used by OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, and others.

sections.title: Morgan's Case — Out of the Loop
sections.summary: Morgan stopped following AI news and stuck with Llama 2 7B. Defense cites rapid model releases in the past quarter. Sentence commuted to community service: attend ThursdAI shows, subscribe, and share with friends.

sections.title: Francisco's Case — Turbulence on Production
sections.summary: Air Canada head of AI rushed chatbot to production using only programmatic assertions. Company lost a legal battle. Guilty of 'turbulence on production.' Highlights the importance of human-in-the-loop evaluation.

sections.title: LLM Evals Refresher — Three Methods
sections.summary: Detailed explanation of LLM evals: compile dataset, run model, score/grade. Three methods: (1) programmatic for numerical outputs, assertions, and code; (2) human-in-the-loop for continuous development evaluation; (3) LLM-as-judge for cost-effective multi-turn grading, still requiring human iteration and bias checking.

sections.title: Maxim's Case — Correct Implementation and Bias Checking
sections.summary: Maxim correctly implemented all three evaluation methods using W&B Weave with continuous evaluation and fast experiments. A prompt injection incident highlights the need to check judges for biases. References Shankar's paper on validating validators and Hamel Hussein's talk. Emphasizes creating custom criteria rather than using off-the-shelf ones.

sections.title: OpenUI Demonstration — Custom Criteria in Practice
sections.summary: Demonstration of OpenUI, an open-source project by W&B co-founder Chris van Pelt, traced and evaluated with W&B Weave. Shows custom criteria (contrast, relevance, polish), version comparison (v16 vs v14 using GPT 3.5 turbo), and multimedia rendering of outputs. Illustrates the importance of a robust evaluation and visualization system.

sections.title: Custom Criteria Exercise — Judging a Conference Talk
sections.summary: Volkov walks through a practical exercise of creating custom evaluation criteria using a conference talk as an example: memorable, educational, helpful, funny, original, clear, articulate, good delivery, and not too promotional. Encourages the audience to apply this approach to their own business apps.

sections.title: Final Case — Alex vs. Maxim
sections.summary: Maximus turns the tables and judges Alex Volkov himself, charging him with 'doubtfully educational content,' interrupting the judge, and 70% promotional content. Found memorable for wearing a wig. Verdict: guilty of 'over commitment to the bit.' Alex closes by inviting attendees to visit the W&B booth, check Weave documentation, and follow ThursdAI.
